after.problem: If $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ with characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-2x-8,$ then ${A}^{3}=$
after.worked_solution:
First, let's divide the polynomial $f(x)={x}^{3}$ by characteristic polynomial $p(x)={x}^{2}-2x-8,$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,x$ | $+$ | $2$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-2x-8\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{3}\,\,}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{3}$ | $-$ | $2{x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $8x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | $2{x}^{2}$ | $+$ | $8x$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  | $2{x}^{2}$ | $-$ | $4x$ | $-$ | $16$ |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $12x$ | $+$ | $16$ |  |  |  |  |

Therefore, we can write ${x}^{3}$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & =q(x)p(x)+(12x+16),\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)=x+2.$  Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
{A}^{3}=q(A)p(A)+(12A+16I).
$$

Now, according to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =q(A)p(A)+(12A+16I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(12A+16I) \\  & =12A+16I.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's start by finding the characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )$:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(\lambda ) & =\text{det}(A-\lambda I) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 11 \\ -3 & -6-\lambda \end{aligned}| \\  & =(6-\lambda )(-6-\lambda )+33 \\  & ={\lambda }^{2}-3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's divide $f(x)$ by $p(x)$ using long division:

|  | $\,\,{x}^{13}$ | $+$ | $x$ |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${x}^{2}-3\,$ | $\,\enclose{longdiv}{{x}^{15}-3{x}^{13}+{x}^{3}-5x+6}$ |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|  | ${x}^{15}$ | $\,\,\,\,-$ | $\,\,\,\,3{x}^{13}$ |  |  |  |  |  |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,5x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,+$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$ |
|  |  |  |  | ${x}^{3}\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,3x$ |  |  |
|  |  |  |  |  | $-\,\,$ | $\,\,2x$ | $\,\,\,\,\,+$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,\,6$ |

Therefore, we can write $f(x)$ as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =q(x)p(x)+r(x) \\  & =q(x)p(x)+(-2x+6)\end{aligned}
$$

where $q(x)={x}^{13}+x.$ Replacing $x$ with $A,$ we have

$$
f(A)=q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I).
$$

According to the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have $p(A)=O.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & =q(A)p(A)+(-2A+6I) \\  & =q(A)\cdot O+(-2A+6I) \\  & =-2A+6I \\  & =-2[\begin{aligned}6 & 11 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}]+6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & -22 \\ 6 & 12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -22 \\ 6 & 18\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's find the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & -3 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )((-4-\lambda )(1-\lambda )+3) & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -1) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{3}+{\lambda }^{2}-7\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the Cayley-Hamilton theorem, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I & =O.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $A$ is invertible, we can multiply this equation by ${A}^{-1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1}({A}^{3}+{A}^{2}-7A+2I) & =O \\ {A}^{2}+A-7I+2{A}^{-1} & =O \\ 2{A}^{-1} & =7I-A-{A}^{2} \\ {A}^{-1} & =\frac{7}{2}I-\frac{1}{2}A-\frac{1}{2}{A}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$
